planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: A rare, pre-industrial Louisiana heirloom also sold as 'Louisiana Hots,' bearing 2-3 inch conical pods that ripen green to orange to red on compact 12-18 inch plants. Thick flesh gives it good drying and powder character with a Tabasco-like flavor and heat a notch above jalapeno. It thrives in Gulf humidity and sets fruit reliably through long hot summers; harvest red for maximum flavor or dry whole pods on the stem for a Cajun-style pepper flake.

common_name: Bell Boy Bell Pepper (Classic Heat-Tolerant AAS Hybrid)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes.

directions: A 1967 All-America Selections winner still sold decades later because it keeps setting four-lobed, thick-walled fruit through summer heat that stalls many other bell peppers. Its large leaf canopy shades fruit from sunscald, a real asset in zone 9a's intense midday sun. Tobacco-mosaic tolerant and reliably productive in containers or raised beds along the Gulf Coast.
sources: MyGardenLife plant library - Bell Pepper Bell Boy

common_name: TAM Mild Habanero Pepper (Texas A&M Low-Pungency Habanero)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant into fertile soil in full sun after frost danger passes.

directions: Released by Texas A&M's South Texas breeding program from a cross of a Yucatan habanero and a heatless Bolivian habanero, bred specifically for the region's heat. It matures about 10 days earlier and out-yields standard orange habanero by roughly 25 percent, carrying full habanero aroma and flavor with only a fraction of the capsaicin, good for cooks who want fruitiness without the burn. It was field-trialed in and performs well under South Texas and Gulf Coast humidity.
sources: ResearchGate - TAM Mild Habanero, a Low-Pungency Habanero Pepper

common_name: Pinot Noir Sweet Pepper (Color-Changing Heat- and Cold-Tolerant Hybrid Bell)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; a good patio or container choice for zone 9a where summer highs regularly exceed the typical bell-pepper fruit-set ceiling.

directions: An ornamental-edible F1 bell pepper bred for a wide performance window, cycling through citrus, berry, lilac, and violet tones before ripening to cherry-red, with foliage and flowering that merely pause rather than abort during the worst heat spikes. The compact habit and striking color stages make it a strong patio or container choice where conventional bells stall out in peak Gulf Coast summer heat. Harvest at any color stage for fresh eating or let fruit fully ripen to red for maximum sweetness.
sources: True Leaf Market - Pinot Noir F1 Hybrid Sweet Pepper
Burpee - Pepper, Sweet, Pinot Noir Hybrid

planting.note: Start extra early indoors, 10-12 weeks before last frost, given notoriously slow germination; needs the longest warm season of the Capsicum chinense types.

directions: A Trinidadian 7 Pot strain that ripens an unusual mustard-green color rather than red, orange, or chocolate, with wrinkled habanero-shaped pods carrying 400,000 to 1,000,000 Scoville units and a fruity, earthy, smoky flavor similar to Yellow 7 Pot. It needs a long, consistently warm season to reach full pod maturity in Gulf Coast gardens. Handle fresh and dried pods with gloves given the extreme heat level.
sources: Tyler Farms - Mustard 7 Pot Pepper Seeds

common_name: Peach Scotch Bonnet Pepper (Caribbean and West African Fruity Superhot)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; vigorous 3-4 foot bushes handle Gulf Coast humidity well, consistent with other chinense Scotch Bonnets already thriving there.

directions: Lantern-shaped pods ripen from green to a distinctive peach or apricot color, carrying 100,000 to 350,000 Scoville units with a mango-apricot fruitiness favored in Caribbean and West African cooking, a natural color-range companion to the chocolate and red Scotch Bonnets already in cultivation. Vigorous bushes handle Gulf humidity well, matching the performance of other chinense Scotch Bonnet types. Harvest fully colored pods for the best balance of fruitiness and heat.
sources: Pepper Joe's - Peach Scotch Bonnet Pepper Seeds
